hlido_opinion.headline: An ambitious open-source MCP server exposing 70 Brazilian public-data sources (533 tools) to AI agents — genuinely useful connective tissue, with unusually careful licensing and acceptable-use disclosures.
hlido_opinion.body: mcp-brasil connects AI agents to Brazilian government and public data — economy, legislation, transparency, judiciary, elections, environment, health, education, public safety, fiscal, aviation — via a single MCP server advertising 533 tools, 131 resources, and 102 prompts across 70 features. The scope is large and the utility is real: getting reliable, structured access to dozens of Brazilian public APIs is exactly the kind of undifferentiated plumbing that makes agents useful in a national context, and 66 of the 70 sources need no API key. What stands out beyond scope is the project's honesty about it: a prominent disclaimer that it is NOT an official government service, MIT covering only the code (each data source keeps its own license), and an explicit Acceptable Use Policy for commercial, journalistic, or decisional use. That posture is exactly right for a tool intermediating sensitive public data. The caveats are inherent to breadth: 533 tools is a lot of surface to keep working as upstream APIs drift, and the review here is repo-health and public-surface, not a live exercise of each connector. Coverage and freshness will live or die on maintenance.

tier_rationale: STEADY reflects a healthy, MIT-licensed repo with documented install, CI, releases, recent commits and real breadth, plus commendable licensing/AUP transparency. Not higher because this is a public-surface + repo-health assessment (medium confidence) — Hlido did not exercise the 533 tools — and a connector aggregator of this size carries ongoing upstream-drift maintenance risk that only sustained activity can retire.
what_it_does_well: Broad, genuinely useful coverage: 70 Brazilian public-data sources through one MCP server
66 of 70 sources require no API key — low friction to start
Exemplary transparency: clear "not an official government service" disclaimer, per-source licensing, published Acceptable Use Policy
MIT-licensed code with documented install, CI, and release history
FastMCP/Python stack that agents (Claude, GPT, Copilot) can consume directly
what_it_fails_at: 533 tools is a large surface to keep functioning as upstream government APIs change
Data freshness and per-connector reliability depend on upstream sources Hlido cannot verify from the repo
Narrow geographic scope — valuable for Brazil, irrelevant elsewhere
No live, browsable demo of the connectors; assessment is repo + stated capability
Per-source data licenses vary, so commercial use requires the buyer to check each one
best_for: Developers building agents that need Brazilian government/public data (compliance, journalism, research, civic tech)
Brazilian civic-tech, legal, and fintech teams wiring public data into LLM workflows
Anyone who wants a single MCP endpoint instead of integrating dozens of public APIs by hand
Research and transparency projects working with subnational fiscal, judicial, or electoral data
not_recommended_for: Teams outside Brazil with no need for Brazilian public data
Use cases requiring an SLA or guaranteed data freshness (this depends on upstream public APIs)
Commercial users unwilling to review each data source's individual license and the AUP
Anyone expecting an official or government-endorsed data pipeline
red_flags: Because it aggregates 70 external public APIs, availability and freshness are only as good as those upstream sources; the project cannot guarantee either, and this review did not exercise the connectors live.
